title: Trail and Landfall
premise: Beatrix Zhou, a railroad engineer who maps abandoned lines to stay ahead of her own past, takes a survey contract on a fogbound coastal spur where the morning tide has exposed a cave the locals have always charged tourists to glimpse—and never enter. Inside, her small expedition finds not treasure but a sealed Victorian railcar holding letters, blueprints, and a confession that could rewrite who built the coast's railways and at what cost. When her employer's backers arrive to strip the cave for salvage, Beatrix must choose between the duty that has kept her moving and the belonging she finds in a town that remembers her grandmother's name. She smuggles the railcar's truth home by rail, testifies at the hearing that decides the cave's fate, and finally stops moving—taking the closed spur line over as its keeper, with the expedition's cartographer, Ilse Marchetti, at her side.
about_author: Emrys Kavanagh is the pen name of a former track surveyor who spent a decade walking decommissioned rail corridors across three continents before turning to fiction. They write from a converted signal box on the northern coast, where the tide still decides the morning's schedule.

chapters.title: The Map of Closed Lines
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She finishes a survey of a dead branch line and is offered a contract on the coastal spur at Greyhaven Head, the one assignment she has avoided for years because her grandmother came from there. She accepts anyway, telling herself it's just another job. Emotional beat: restless avoidance dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: Arrival at Low Water
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She arrives in the shrinking town of Greyhaven, where the stationmaster, old Tom Ferris, recognizes her surname and says nothing—yet. She walks the crumbling spur and notices the tide has pulled back farther than the charts allow, exposing dark rock below the cliff. Emotional beat: the past arriving before she does.

chapters.title: The Cave That Charges Admission
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. In the harbor pub, she hears the legend: a sea cave that appears once in a generation, which locals have sold tickets to glimpse but never entered, on pain of bad luck. Ilse Marchetti, a cartographer hired by the same backers, sketches the coastline and asks too many good questions. Emotional beat: curiosity kindling against instinct.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gives Back
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Ilse's alternating POV. At dawn the cave mouth stands open. Beatrix surveys it professionally while something in her grandmother's letters—found in chapter one's packing—itches at her memory. Ilse notices Beatrix flinch at the name Zhou chalked inside the entrance. Emotional beat: the first crack in her invisibility.

chapters.title: The Expedition Forms
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Her employer, Halloway Salvage, sends a crew: pragmatic divers, a lawyer named Cray who reads contracts aloud at breakfast, and drones that map what eyes can't. Beatrix realizes she's not leading a survey; she's the front for a salvage claim. Emotional beat: complicity settling in like wet gravel.

chapters.title: First Descent
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. The team enters the cave at slack tide, racing the water. Ilse maps the passages and finds tool marks—deliberate, engineered cuts, not erosion. Beatrix goes quiet when the tunnel geometry matches a spur line that officially never existed. Emotional beat: wonder shadowed by the sense of walking into someone's secret.

chapters.title: The Railcar
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Deep in the cave, sealed behind a collapse the Victorians engineered on purpose, the team finds an intact railcar: letters, blueprints, pay ledgers, and a confession signed by the line's chief engineer—her great-grandfather—admitting the coastal railway was built with falsified surveys that cost lives in a flood. Emotional beat: inheritance turning to weight.

chapters.title: Cray Reads the Fine Print
chapters.summary: Cray's POV. The salvage claim covers 'recoverable artifacts of commercial value'—which means the railcar, the blueprints, and the story. Beatrix realizes the confession could also void Halloway's claim and protect the cave, if it ever surfaces. She pockets one letter and lies badly about it. Emotional beat: the first open act of betrayal against duty.

chapters.title: Tom Ferris Remembers
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The stationmaster tells Beatrix about her grandmother, who left Greyhaven in disgrace after the flood, carrying the family's shame inland. He shows Beatrix a wall of names from the disaster—three of them Zhou. Emotional beat: belonging offered by someone with no agenda but memory.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. A storm system stalls offshore; the tides that opened the cave will close it violently and may collapse the cliff—and the town's seawall—within two weeks. Halloway orders a full extraction before then. Beatrix's hidden letter becomes a ticking liability. Emotional beat: time compressing, choices sharpening.

chapters.title: Ilse Asks the Wrong Question
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse confronts Beatrix on the cliff path: why did a Zhou flinch inside a cave her family never officially touched? Beatrix deflects, and the distance between them—professional warmth shading into something more—turns cold. Emotional beat: love against duty, first real cost.

chapters.title: The Letter She Shouldn't Have
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Reading her great-grandfather's confession by lamplight, she finds a second document: proof he tried to stop the flood and was silenced by the railway company—the same company Halloway's founders came from. The truth isn't shame; it's exoneration. Emotional beat: grief reframing into purpose.

chapters.title: Sabotage, or Safety?
chapters.summary: Cray's POV. Cray discovers the missing letter and gives Beatrix an ultimatum: return it or be removed from the expedition—and blacklisted from every rail contract in the country. Beatrix, who has survived by staying invisible, faces the end of the only life she built. Emotional beat: the price of stopping, made explicit.

chapters.title: Night on the Spur
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Ilse's alternating POV. Beatrix tells Ilse everything—the family, the confession, the theft. Instead of turning her in, Ilse proposes a plan: document the railcar publicly as heritage, not salvage, using Beatrix's engineering authority and Ilse's maps. They kiss in the signal box. Emotional beat: alliance becoming love.

chapters.title: The Town Decides
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. Beatrix addresses the harbor pub, laying out what the cave holds and what Halloway will take. Half the town wants the money; the other half wants the names restored. Tom casts the deciding voice for heritage, invoking the flood dead. Emotional beat: a community choosing memory over coin.

chapters.title: Halloway Moves Early
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Cray's crew enters the cave at night, ahead of the storm, to strip the railcar. Beatrix and Ilse follow, and in the dark passages a diver's lamp starts a minor collapse that seals the inner chamber—with Cray and the railcar on the wrong side of it. Emotional beat: panic, and the terrible arithmetic of rescue.

chapters.title: Against the Incoming Tide
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Using the spur's old maintenance tunnel—her great-grandfather's own escape route—Beatrix leads a rescue through flooded workings as the tide turns. She reaches Cray, who is injured and trapped beside the railcar, and pulls him out with the confession still inside. Emotional beat: duty and love finally pulling the same direction.

chapters.title: The Cave Closes
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. As the storm peaks, the sea seals the cave mouth for another generation. The railcar's contents are safe on land; the chamber itself is beyond anyone's reach. Cray, saved by the woman he threatened, quietly amends the salvage claim to a heritage designation. Emotional beat: awe, exhaustion, the strange mercy of the sea.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. In the county hall, Beatrix testifies—reading her great-grandfather's confession aloud, naming the flood dead, including her family. Halloway's backers withdraw rather than be associated with the original cover-up. The spur and the headland are granted protected status. Emotional beat: truth spoken at last, and surviving it.

chapters.title: Reopening the Line
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. With the heritage grant comes an unexpected offer: the closed spur can be restored as a coastal heritage railway, and the town wants a Zhou to run it. Beatrix, who has never stayed anywhere longer than a contract, signs her name to a place. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: Landfall
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Spring comes to Greyhaven. Ilse finishes the definitive map of the cave—drawn from memory and the blueprints—and frames it in the station house beside the wall of flood names, the Zhoos restored among them. Beatrix and Ilse take the first test run down the reopened spur at dawn. Emotional beat: home, finally, in motion and at rest.

chapters.title: The Keeper of the Spur
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Epilogue: a year on, tourists pay admission again—but this time to ride the line and hear the true story Beatrix tells herself, every departure, from the driver's seat. A letter arrives from a stranger claiming another sealed chamber on another dead line. Beatrix smiles, files it, and stays. Emotional beat: the ending of running, and the beginning of keeping.
